title: How To PROPERLY Barbell Row For A Bigger Back (Stop Making These Mistakes!)
description:
If you've always wanted to boost your back thickness and back width, you need to learn how to do barbell rows. Unfortunately, most people butcher the barbell row technique (or “bent over row”). If you don't know how to barbell row with proper form, you're shortchanging yourself on potential muscle gains. Also, you're putting yourself at risk of severe injuries. In this video, I'll guide you through the barbell row form, step-by-step so that you can follow along.

The barbell bent-over row works the whole back. But the main muscles activated will be the latissimus dorsi (lats), the traps (both middle and lower), and the rear deltoids. If you execute the bent-over barbell row with proper form, you should mainly feel these areas of your back working as you pull the weight. 

There are three stages to the barbell row technique: the starting position, the concentric rowing movement, and the eccentric rowing movement. When it comes to the starting position, many gym-goers commit two mistakes. The first is that they perform the barbell row too upright – this emphasizes the upper traps, instead of the back. The second is going too low such that the back rounds; the back should remain neutral throughout the exercise.

The mistakes don't end there either. When it comes to the concentric rowing movement, many people tend to flare the elbows out excessively. As a result, they put their shoulders in a compromised position. The second mistake during this portion is letting the shoulders roll forward – once again, this puts the shoulders in a compromised position. There's a third as well: many people tend to excessively round the back when rowing; this places significant stress on the lower back.

Last but not least, there are two mistakes associated with the eccentric portion of the exercise. The first is allowing the back to round and to fall out of proper alignment. The second is simply dropping the weight – this negatively impacts your muscle hypertrophy potential.

Just remember that while fundamental exercises, like the barbell row, are great for building muscle, their effectiveness relies on how you perform them. Proper execution of exercises will prevent severe injuries and enable you to build muscle faster. And not to mention, in the right areas.

segments.text: The Barbell Roe was one of the most effective exercises of building a wider, thicker back.

However, this exercise is also one that many people get wrong, which is not only detrimental

back.
But luckily, in this video, I'll go through a step-by-step tutorial showing you exactly
how to perform the Barbell Roe from maximal back growth.
First off, let's take a look at the muscles worked.
Although the whole back muscle trail will be worked, the main muscles targeted will be
the lats, the mid and lower traps, and the rear delts.
You want to mainly feel these areas of your back working as you pull the weight.
But as you'll see in this video, by tweaking your form, you'll be able to emphasize certain
back muscles more than others.
And do note that the lower back will also be heavily involved as it's going to contract
asymmetrically throughout the movement, so you'll feel attention there as well.
With that being said, let's get into how exactly to perform the Barbell Roe.
First, let's start with how to optimally set up the Barbell Roe, which, as you'll see,
will vary depending on both your individual anatomy and your goals.
To begin, get your feet set upright by placing them slightly wider than hip width, but narrower
than shoulder width.
But experiment with this, as taller individuals often do better with a wider stance.
You can also rotate your feet outward slightly if this makes the movement more comfortable
for you.
When looking down, the bar should lay over your midfoot to toe area.
Next, it's time to grip the bar.
As a general rule, grip the bar just outside the width of your knees, but you definitely
want to experiment with a slightly wider or slightly narrower grip depending on your
goals and what feels most comfortable for you.
For instance, a wider grip will enable you to both pull the bar higher towards the sternum
and flare the elbows out more, which will as a result hit more of the traps.
Your rear delts and your overall upper back muscles do do the greater transverse extension
of both.
Whereas the narrower shoulder width grip will enable you to both pull the bar lower towards
your belly button and tuck the elbows closer to your sides, which now puts the lats in
a more mechanical advantageous position due to the greater shoulder extension involved
and therefore prioritizes its development instead.
And similarly, as for whether you should grip overhand or underhand, an underhand grip
will enable you to tuck the elbows even closer to your sides and hence prioritize the lats
even more.
But it does come at the cost of greater biceps involvement.
And as shown in the following graph, this was actually analyzed and confirmed in an extensive

most balanced back development.

forearms to come out of proper alignment and lead to increased wrist and elbow stress.
And at the same time, you want to also avoid going too wide to the point where your elbows
have to excessively flare out.
In this video, I'm going to stick to using a wider overhand grip, but just note that the
same steps and tips apply for whatever grip variation you choose to use.
Next, we want to get into the starting position of the rope.

to keep the back neutral as you do so.
From here, push your hips back out while just very slightly bending the knees while lowering
the barbell down.
You want to stop at the point where it feels like your hamstring flexibility limits you from
going down any further without rounding your back.
For most people, this is going to be somewhere around a 15 to 45 degree angle as shown here.
But as your flexibility improves and you become more proficient with the movement, you
can gradually attempt to get more parallel to the ground for a greater range of motion
to more effectively work the back.
Some things to avoid when getting into the starting position are to avoid performing the
movement to upright, as this is going to emphasize more of the upper traps as opposed
to the back due to now resembling more of a shrug movement pattern.
And avoid going past your end range of hamstring flexibility by getting too low to the point

Once you're in the starting position, that's it for the setup and you're now ready

Advocates to avoid as you row are to avoid pulling the bar too high and flaring the elbows

Avoid excessively rounding your back as you row.
Instead, keep your chest up and core engaged to maintain a neutral back.
Avoid internally rotating shoulder by letting it roll forward as you pull, as this puts

Instead, lighten the weight and focus on pulling the shoulders back and squeezing the shoulder

Once you successfully row the weight up, it's time for the descent back to the starting position.

As you lower the weight, you want to let your scapula naturally protract outwards like so

Some things to avoid during the descent are to avoid letting your back round and fall
